title: Compare probabilities from a model with observed frequencies and explain any differences

sections.skill: Compare probabilities from a model with observed frequencies and explain any differences

questions.skill: Compare probabilities from a model with observed frequencies and explain any differences
questions.prompt: A fair number cube is rolled 60 times, and a 5 comes up 14 times. How many 5s does the model predict? How does the observed count compare?
questions.prompt_markup:
A fair number cube is rolled 60 times, and a 5 comes up 14 times.
How many 5s does the model predict? How does the observed count compare?
questions.correct_answer: The model predicts 10 fives; the observed 14 is 4 more than expected.
questions.grading_note: Grade both: 10 expected, and the comparison with 14.

questions.skill: Compare probabilities from a model with observed frequencies and explain any differences
questions.prompt: A coin is claimed to be fair. It is flipped 100 times and lands heads 61 times. Compare this with the model. Give a possible reason for the difference.
questions.prompt_markup:
A coin is claimed to be fair. It is flipped 100 times and lands heads 61 times.
Compare this with the model. Give a possible reason for the difference.
questions.correct_answer: The model predicts about 50 heads. Random variation can explain some of the difference, but 61 heads might also mean the coin is not fair.
questions.grading_note: Any answer that compares with the expected 50 and gives a reasonable cause (chance variation or an unfair coin).

questions.skill: Compare probabilities from a model with observed frequencies and explain any differences
questions.prompt: A spinner has 4 equal sections, one of them yellow. In 80 spins, it lands on yellow 35 times. Which conclusion is best?
questions.prompt_markup:
A spinner has 4 equal sections, one of them yellow. In 80 spins, it lands on yellow 35 times.
Which conclusion is best?

choices.text: Yellow came up much more than the expected 20 times, so the spinner may not be fair.
Yellow should come up 35 times in every 80 spins.
The results match the model exactly.

questions.correct_answer: Yellow came up much more than the expected 20 times, so the spinner may not be fair.

sections.skill: Judge whether a result is consistent with a model by using a simulation

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Judge whether a result is consistent with a model by using a simulation
questions.standard_level: High school (Common Core high-school standard; this bank places it at Grade 9 as a second forward step. This is an instructional choice, not an official grade assignment.)
questions.prompt: A spinner is claimed to land on red 25% of the time. The dot plot shows the number of reds in each of 50 simulated sets of 20 spins under that model. A real spinner lands on red 11 times in 20 spins. Is the result consistent with the model? Use the simulation.
questions.prompt_markup:
A spinner is claimed to land on red 25% of the time. The dot plot shows the number of reds in each of 50 simulated sets of 20 spins under that model. A real spinner lands on red 11 times in 20 spins.
Is the result consistent with the model? Use the simulation.
questions.correct_answer: No. 11 or more reds never happened in the 50 simulations, so the result casts doubt on the 25% model.

figure.description: Dot plot titled "Number of reds in 20 spins (50 simulations)", number line from 0 to 12. Dots per value: 1: 1, 2: 3, 3: 6, 4: 9, 5: 11, 6: 9, 7: 6, 8: 3, 9: 1, 10: 1.

data.xlabel: Number of reds in 20 spins (50 simulations)
